Lots of great updates on the site in the past couple days as I've been working through all of the gaps we've had over the years. Generally the big work has been done, but we just need to iron out the details (as with BE and DLL builds). Getting rid of Boost, and the other dependencies over time, made all of it a LOT easier.

elements.text: Turns out there was an integer version of the std::stream-based number parser in use in several places in the client-server interfaces, and it has the same flaw. every thread passed thru a critical section. Also the json parser had a dumb perf flaw. And the http serializer was sending header and body independently. With that and one io scheduler optimization, the perf is back to pre-boost-removal baseline, with significant improvement in many regions (almost 2x in some case). Also building with the verbose logging level disabled increase http server performance at every level by about 10%.

text:
Thanks, this is nice work. I checked it against `bs --settings` on current master and against the parser source. Nearly every default matches. Here’s what doesn’t:
*Defaults*
• `database.path` defaults to `mainnet`, not `bitcoin`. The default store directory is named for the network (`./mainnet`, `./testnet4`). A configured path gets `/<network>` appended, so `path = bitcoin` means `bitcoin/mainnet`. (The reference page was corrected after your snapshot.)
• The bucket counts of `header`, `tx`, `ins`, `outs`, `pool` and `wtxid` aren’t fixed values. bs derives them from each table’s `expected` count and the installed memory. The load factor is 7.5 at 8 GB or less and 2.5 at 32 GB or more, linear in between, and 50 to 5 for `outs`. `strong.buckets` follows `tx.expected`. The counts in your snapshot (e.g. header 385,181) are what a 32 GB+ machine derives. So leave them unset unless the user is deliberately sizing, and present them as “derived” rather than as defaults.
• `peer.user_agent`, `electrum.server_name` and `sparrow.server_name` default to the build’s version string, so a fixed `/libbitcoin:4.0.10255/` will differ on any other build. Treat these as “empty means the built-in value” rather than as a literal.
• `node.minimum_fee_rate`: bs now prints `0.000001`. That changed recently, and the parser reads any valid form, so `1e-06` works too.
• Settings missing from the catalog:
    ◦ `credential` in `[admin]`, `[native]`, `[electrum]`, `[sparrow]` and `[esplora]`;
    ◦ `cert_auth` and `key_pass` in `[electrum]` and `[sparrow]`;
    ◦ `bitcoin.signet_challenge`;
    ◦ `forks.signet`.
*Exposed-interface warning.* Your “exposed interface without credentials” warning checks only the credential and TLS fields the catalog has. For the services missing `credential`, a user can’t add a login, so only the TLS fields can clear it. The warning also clears when any one field is filled (e.g. `key_pass` alone), which doesn’t secure anything. It would be better to require a complete TLS pair (`cert_path` + `key_path`) or a `credential`. Note that bs describes `credential` as “not secure” without TLS.
*Using `--settings` as the source.* The values `bs -s` prints are the ones in effect: network defaults, derived bucket counts and configured values (marked `# configured`). The “defaults to …” text in the descriptions currently always shows mainnet values, even under `-n`, and the derived buckets say “dynamic default”. Both are being fixed so the descriptions show the network’s and machine’s actual defaults. Until then, take the values, not the description text, from `bs -n <net> -s`.
*Network selection* (current behavior; this area is still subject to change)
• `[bitcoin] network = testnet4` resets every default to that network’s values, then applies what the file sets. The generator diffs against mainnet defaults instead. So a value that happens to equal the mainnet default is left out of the file, and bs uses the testnet value. Example: setting `inbound.bind` to port 8333 on testnet4 writes nothing, and bs binds 48333.
• For the same reason, the “milestone-network-mismatch” danger warning doesn’t apply. With `network = testnet4` and no milestone in the file, bs uses the testnet4 milestone.
• The store hint `bs -n testnet4` isn’t needed. `bs --config bs.cfg` creates the store if it’s missing, and `-m`/`--make` creates it without running. If the file sets `database.path`, running `bs -n testnet4` without the file creates a different store from the one the file points to.
*Settings fixed at store creation.* The bucket counts, the network, chain parameters, forks, milestone, `interval_depth`, `limited_blocks`, `silent_start_height` and whether filters are enabled are all captured when the store is created. An existing store’s values override the file, and each override is logged. Your fixed-at-creation notices are right in spirit. The full list is at <https://libbitcoin.org/configuration/#10-settings-fixed-at-store-creation|libbitcoin.org/configuration#…>
*Milestone wording*
• Below the milestone bs performs identity verification: it makes sure you get the blocks you asked for. Above it, blocks are fully validated. It isn’t assume-valid, which is partial validation. So validation doesn’t “start at” the milestone, and the `maximum_height` warning built on that idea should be reworded or dropped.
*Presets*
• Tor privacy: `node.provide_privacy` is BIP324 opportunistic encryption, unrelated to Tor (fine to turn on, but don’t describe it as Tor privacy). The preset also leaves inbound listening on clearnet. A Tor setup would normally also disable or restrict inbound and set `manual.socks`.
• The wallet, Sparrow and explorer presets bind `0.0.0.0` without TLS. Your warning catches this, but a loopback default with a note on exposing it would be safer.
• The genesis-validation preset (`milestone = <genesis>:0`) matches the docs. The default checkpoints still apply. They are consensus, not a shortcut: remove them only if you want to follow Bitcoin Core’s hard fork, and the performance difference is largely inconsequential.

I’ve verified the `portable config` idea I mentioned in the meeting. There were the two expected address settings that didn’t get default ports (hosts and origins). I’ve generalized those, so we will be able to set up a single config file that manages all networks, assuming the intent is to keep them in sync. A `self` takes the network’s default p2p port, not the bound port.

I think this will hold up for our community servers. So 2 config files on 2 machines, vs. 10 total. I ran across the idea accidentally, as I noticed I was able to do this unintentionally with no problems. The trick is to just accept the default ports, and default everything that’s network specific.
